name: The Hall of Honest Failure
goal: Read a traceback, locate the failing line, and isolate a fault without guessing.

description.what: What Python prints when a program fails, how to read it, how a failure found while the file is being read differs from one found while it is running, the handful of failures a beginner actually meets by name, and how to find a fault by probing a program rather than by staring at it.
description.why: Most of a programmer's day is spent with a broken program, and the difference between somebody who can learn alone and somebody who cannot is whether the error message is information or noise; a learner who guesses at fixes is not debugging but shuffling, and they will still be shuffling in a year.
description.enables: You will be able to read a traceback from the bottom upwards, say what kind of failure it was and which line stopped, tell a failure found before the program ran from one found partway through, name the commonest failures from their messages, and narrow a wrong answer down to the line that produced it by printing values as the program runs.
description.assumes: The five floors before this one: that a program is a file of instructions run from top to bottom, that names refer to values and values have types, that arithmetic and conversion can be written out, that `if` chooses between paths, and that `while` and `for` repeat work.
description.assessed: You will read tracebacks and say what they mean, predict what a probed program prints, repair broken whole programs whose fault is not on the line the message names, and explain in prose how you would corner a fault you cannot yet see.

sections.title: Read it from the bottom
sections.body:
When a program fails, Python does not sulk. It prints a **traceback**, which is a short report of what went wrong and where, and it is the most useful thing on the screen. Beginners scroll past it because it looks like wreckage. It is not wreckage; it is the answer.

Read it **from the bottom upwards**. The last line always has the same shape: a name, a colon, and a message. The name is the **kind** of failure - `ZeroDivisionError` here - and the message is Python's one-sentence account of it. That single line tells you what happened, and only when you know what happened is it worth asking where.

Now go up one line. The line beginning `File` gives the **number** of the line at which the program stopped, and under it Python reprints that line of your source with an arrow beneath the part that failed. So the bottom line says what, and the two lines above it say where. Everything further up is context you do not need yet.

One more thing is worth noticing, and it is easy to miss: `starting` was printed. The program really did run lines 1, 2 and 3 before it fell over on line 4. Output that appeared before the traceback is evidence of how far the program got, and it costs nothing to read.
sections.code:
total = 30
count = 0
print("starting")
average = total / count
print("average is", average)

annotations.text: Nothing is wrong with this line and Python will never complain about it. A count of zero only becomes a problem two lines later, when something tries to divide by it.
This runs, and `starting` appears on the screen. When you read the traceback afterwards, that word is proof that the program reached line 3.
The line the traceback names. Python worked out `total / count`, found the divisor was zero, and stopped here.
This line never runs at all. A traceback marks the end of the program: nothing below the failing line happens.

checkpoint.prompt:
Running the program above prints `starting` and then this:

`Traceback (most recent call last):`
`  File "prog.py", line 4, in <module>`
`    average = total / count`
`ZeroDivisionError: division by zero`

Fill in what the traceback tells you.
checkpoint.template:
kind of failure: ___
line of the program that stopped: ___
checkpoint.explain: The last line names the kind of failure and the `File` line above it gives the number. People reach for the number first because a line number feels more concrete, but knowing that you stopped on line 4 without knowing why tells you nothing at all about what to change.

sections.title: Broken before it starts
sections.body:
There are two quite different moments at which a program can fail, and telling them apart costs nothing and saves a great deal.

Before running anything, Python reads the whole file and checks that it is legal Python. If it is not, you get a **syntax error**, and here is the part that matters: **not one line of your program runs**. No output appears. A missing colon after `while`, a bracket you never closed, a quotation mark left open - all of these are found by reading, not by running.

If the file is legal, Python starts at line 1 and runs it. A failure discovered now is a **runtime error**, and by definition the program was already going: the lines above the failure ran, and whatever they printed is on the screen. So the presence or absence of output is a free diagnosis. Nothing printed at all, and a message with no `Traceback` line above it, means the file never ran. Some output and then `Traceback` means it ran and stumbled.

The arrow in a syntax error marks the point where Python got **stuck**, which is at or after your mistake and never before it. Below, the mistake is a missing `)` at the end of line 2, and Python reports line 2 - because it read on past the end of that line looking for the closing bracket and only then gave up. Older Pythons, and many other languages, report the line **after** instead, which is why the advice is always the same: start at the arrow and read upwards until you reach a line that makes sense on its own.

annotations.text: Perfectly good, and it still never runs. `one` does not appear on the screen, because the file was rejected before line 1 was reached.
The mistake. There is no `)` at the end, so the opening bracket is never closed, and Python reports `SyntaxError: '(' was never closed` against this line.
Where your eye probably went first, because this is where the program stops looking sensible. There is nothing to fix here.
Unreachable for a reason that has nothing to do with itself. Every line of a file with a syntax error in it is unreachable.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill in the names of the two moments at which a program can fail.
checkpoint.template:
A ___ error is found while Python is reading the file, so no line of the program runs and nothing is printed.
A ___ error is found while Python is running the file, so the lines above it ran and their output is on the screen.
checkpoint.explain: The distinction halves your search before you have read a word of the message: output on the screen proves the file was legal Python, so no amount of hunting through the brackets and colons can help you there.

sections.title: The failures you will actually meet
sections.body:
Python has a great many kinds of failure, and you will meet about five of them for months. Learn these by their messages and most tracebacks stop being frightening.

- `NameError` - you used a name that nothing was ever assigned to. Nearly always a typo, or a name assigned inside a branch that did not run.
- `TypeError` - you asked for an operation the types do not support, such as adding a number to a piece of text. The message names both types, which is usually the whole diagnosis.
- `ValueError` - the type was right but the value was not. `int("twelve")` is the classic: text is exactly what `int` wants, and `twelve` is not a number it can read.
- `ZeroDivisionError` - something divided by a value that turned out to be zero. The fault is almost never the division; it is whatever made the divisor zero.
- `IndentationError` - the spaces at the start of a line do not line up with the block above.

One more arrives the moment you have somewhere to keep many values at once: `IndexError`, meaning you asked for the fifth thing out of three. That belongs to a later floor and is named here only so it is familiar when it turns up.

Two habits pay off immediately. First, **read the message, not just the name** - `invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'twelve'` hands you the offending value in quotes. Second, ask what the failure is **evidence** of. A `TypeError` on a line that looks perfectly correct is usually evidence that a name further up is holding something other than what you assumed.
sections.code:
print("How many potions?")
raw = "twelve"
count = int(raw)
print(count * 2)

annotations.text: Runs, prints, and is entirely innocent. It is here so that you see output above the traceback and know from that alone that the file was legal.
The real fault, about which Python says nothing. `raw` is holding a piece of text that spells a number in words.

The line the traceback names: `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'twelve'`. The kind of thing handed to `int` was right; the value inside it was not, and the message quotes it back at you.
Never runs. Had `raw` been `"12"`, this line would have printed 24.

checkpoint.prompt: Give the name of the failure Python reports in each of these four situations. Spell each one exactly as Python does.
checkpoint.template:
adding the number 1 to a piece of text: ___
asking int for the number in the text "seven": ___
reading a name that was never assigned: ___
dividing by a count that turned out to be zero: ___
checkpoint.explain: The pair worth separating is the first two. One is about the kind of thing you handed over and the other is about what was inside it: `int` refuses text that spells a word, not because text is the wrong kind of thing - text is exactly what it expects - but because that particular text is not a number.

sections.title: Probing, not guessing
sections.body:
The harder failures do not crash. The program runs to the end, reports nothing, and prints the wrong answer - and there is no traceback to read, because as far as Python is concerned nothing went wrong. Now you have to find the fault yourself, and there is a method.

**Reproduce it first.** Find an exact input that fails every time, and write it down. A fault you cannot make happen on demand is a fault you cannot tell you have fixed, and the commonest waste of an afternoon is repairing something that was never broken.

**Then narrow it.** You know the answer is wrong at the end and right at the start, so the fault lies somewhere between. Put a `print` roughly halfway and look: if the values are already wrong there, the fault is above it; if they are still right, it is below. Each probe halves what is left, so a program of any size falls in a handful of steps. Probes that say which values they are showing - `print("probe: n is", n)` - are worth the extra typing, because six bare numbers down the screen tell you nothing.

**And change one thing at a time.** Change three, and a run that comes out right leaves you not knowing which one mattered, while a run that comes out wrong leaves you worse off than you started. Change one, run the same input, compare. Then take the probes out - they were scaffolding, not code.
sections.code:
total = 0
n = 1
while n <= 5:
    print("probe: n is", n, "and total is", total)
    total = total + n
    n = n + 1
print("sum is", total)

annotations.text: The line most likely to be wrong in a loop like this, and the reason for the probe. `<=` and `<` differ by exactly one pass, and so the answer differs by exactly the last number.
The probe. It names both values it shows, so the output can be read without counting lines, and it sits at the top of the body so it reports the state the pass was given.
Compare what this line does against the probe printed at the start of the next pass. That comparison is the whole technique.
The real output. When the probes have done their job this should be the only line still printing.

checkpoint.prompt: A probe has been put inside this loop. What does the program print? Write all four lines.
checkpoint.code:
n = 1
while n < 4:
    print("probe", n)
    n = n + 1
print("done", n)
checkpoint.explain: The last line is what a probe is for. The loop stops at 4 because the condition is tested before each pass, so the name is left holding the first value that failed the test rather than the last one that passed it. Printing after the loop as well as inside it shows you that instead of leaving it to be argued about.

guided-practice.prompt:
A learner runs this program:

`gold = 40`
`share = 0`
`print("dividing")`
`each = gold / share`
`print(each)`

and Python answers:

`dividing`
`Traceback (most recent call last):`
`  File "prog.py", line 4, in <module>`
`    each = gold / share`
`ZeroDivisionError: division by zero`

Read the traceback from the bottom upwards and fill in the three blanks.
guided-practice.template:
kind of failure: ___
line of the program that stopped: ___
line of the program that actually needs changing: ___
guided-practice.hint: The last line names the failure and the `File` line above it gives the number that stopped. Then ask which earlier line decided that `share` would be zero.
guided-practice.explain: The third blank is what separates reading a traceback from using one. Line 4 is where Python stopped and it is written perfectly correctly; the reason it could not run is a decision made two lines earlier, and no amount of rewriting the division will help.

guided-practice.prompt: A traceback has just appeared on your screen. Put these four questions into the order in which you should ask them.
fragments: What kind of failure was it?
Which line of my program stopped?
What were the values on that line at that moment?
Which earlier line put a wrong value there?
guided-practice.hint: This is the traceback read from its bottom line upwards, and then one step further back into the program.
guided-practice.explain: The tempting order starts with the line number, because that is the most concrete thing on the screen. It is also the least useful on its own: the kind of failure tells you what sort of wrong value to go looking for, and without it you are staring at a correct line wondering what is wrong with it.

guided-practice.prompt: Two programs are run. The first prints `loading` and then stops with an error message. The second prints nothing whatsoever and stops with an error message. Only one of them can possibly contain a missing bracket or a missing colon. Say which, and explain how the output alone tells you.
guided-practice.hint: Ask when each kind of failure is discovered: while Python is reading the file, or while it is running it.
guided-practice.explain: It is the second, and the reasoning runs backwards from the output: a syntax error is found before line 1 runs, so a program that printed anything at all was legal Python and its brackets and colons are all present. The first program's fault is a runtime one, and hunting for it in the punctuation is time spent searching a room the fault cannot be in.

guided-practice.prompt: This program reads two typed lines - a total, then a count - and prints `average is 7.5` for the typed lines `30` and `4`. When the count is `0` it should instead print `no items` and nothing else. At the moment that case stops the program with a traceback naming line 3. Repair it.
guided-practice.starterCode:
total = int(input())
count = int(input())
print("average is", total / count)
guided-practice.hint: The traceback names the division, but the division itself is written correctly. Decide what should happen for the value that makes it impossible, and decide it before any dividing takes place.
guided-practice.explain: The fourth test is the one that catches a half-repair. A guard written as `if total == 0` also passes the third test, because that case happens to have a zero in it as well, and only a case with a zero total and a count above zero separates the two. Guarding the divisor is the fix; guarding whatever else happened to be zero is a coincidence.

guided-practice.prompt: This program should read a whole number and count down from it, printing each number on its own line and then `launch`. For the typed line `3` it prints `3`, `2`, `1`, `launch`. At the moment it prints nothing at all - not even the first number - and reports a syntax error. Repair it.
guided-practice.starterCode:
count = int(input())
while count > 0
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("launch")
guided-practice.solution:
count = int(input())
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("launch")
guided-practice.hint: Nothing printed means the file never ran, so the fault is punctuation rather than arithmetic. Python's message is `expected ':'` and its arrow sits at the end of a line.
guided-practice.explain: The absence of output is the diagnosis here rather than an extra misfortune: had the countdown printed `3` and then failed, the fault could not have been a missing colon, because the file would already have been read and accepted. The negative test matters because a repair that turns the condition round would still print nothing for `-4` while failing everything else.

guided-practice.prompt: This program reads a whole number and should print the sum of every whole number from 1 up to and including it, so for the typed line `5` it prints `15`. It reports no error at all and prints `10`. Put a probe inside the loop, compare what it shows against what you expected, and repair the program.
guided-practice.starterCode:
n = int(input())
total = 0
count = 1
while count < n:
    total = total + count
    count = count + 1
print(total)
guided-practice.solution:
n = int(input())
total = 0
count = 1
while count <= n:
    total = total + count
    count = count + 1
print(total)
guided-practice.hint: Print `count` and `total` at the top of the loop body, run it for the typed line `5`, and ask which value of `count` never appears.
guided-practice.explain: The gap between 15 and 10 is exactly 5, which is the loudest possible hint that the last pass never happened - and a probe makes that visible instead of merely inferred. The `1` test kills the wrong repair of starting `count` at 0, since that adds a harmless zero and still gives 15 for the first case.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a program that reads one typed line holding a whole number and prints one divided by that number. For the typed line `4` it prints `0.25`. There is exactly one whole number for which the division cannot be done at all; when that one is typed, print `cannot divide` and nothing else.
guided-practice.starterCode:
n = int(input())
# Exactly one value of n makes the division impossible.
# Send that one value down a different path first.
guided-practice.hint: Work out for yourself which typed line would reproduce the failure, then send that case down a different path before the division is reached.
guided-practice.explain: This is a fault found on purpose rather than by accident: you are asked which input breaks it, which is exactly the question you must ask of somebody else's bug report. The `1` test is worth a second look, because `1 / 1` prints `1.0` and not `1` - division always produces a number with a point, whatever it divides.

independent-practice.prompt: This program reads three typed lines - an item's name, its price in whole pence, and how many were bought - and should print `lantern costs 120` for the lines `lantern`, `40` and `3`. It stops with a traceback naming line 4, and line 4 is written correctly. Repair it.
independent-practice.starterCode:
item = input()
price = input()
count = input()
print(item, "costs", price * count)
independent-practice.solution:
item = input()
price = int(input())
count = int(input())
print(item, "costs", price * count)
independent-practice.explain: The message says that the two things being multiplied cannot be multiplied, and the line it names is the only line that could have said so - yet the values it complains about were decided two and three lines earlier. Repairing only one of those lines is worse than repairing neither, because a number multiplied by text quietly repeats the text instead of failing, and you get an answer with no warning at all.

independent-practice.prompt: This program reads a whole number and should print `even` when the number divides by two exactly and `odd` when it does not. For the typed line `4` it prints `odd`. It reports no error. Repair it.
independent-practice.explain: Every answer is exactly the wrong way round, and that shape is worth recognising: a fault that is wrong for every input lives in the decision itself rather than in some awkward case. Printing the remainder beside the answer settles in a single run whether the arithmetic or the labelling is at fault, and the negative case is here because the remainder of a negative number is not always what people assume.

independent-practice.prompt: This program reads a number of players and then a number of biscuits, and prints two lines: `each 3` and then `left 1` for the typed lines `4` and `13`. Its author tried it on a dozen deliveries and never saw it fail. One of the cases below stops it dead. Repair it so that case prints `no players` and nothing else.
independent-practice.starterCode:
players = int(input())
biscuits = int(input())
print("each", biscuits // players)
print("left", biscuits % players)
independent-practice.solution:
players = int(input())
biscuits = int(input())
if players == 0:
    print("no players")
else:
    print("each", biscuits // players)
    print("left", biscuits % players)
independent-practice.explain: A fault nobody has seen is still a fault, and the reason this one hid for a dozen deliveries is that it needs one particular value rather than an unusual combination. Notice too that the broken version prints nothing at all before it stops, even though the failing line is the third: Python works out what to print before it prints anything, so the whole line is lost.

independent-practice.prompt: A market stall closes for the day and adds up. Write a program that reads two typed lines - how many items were sold, then how much was taken in whole pence - and prints one line, `price 40`, giving what a single item cost in whole pence. On days when nothing at all was sold it prints `nothing sold` and nothing else.
independent-practice.explain: The last case is the interesting one and it is not a misprint: a day with money taken and nothing sold is nonsense, and the program is told to report the count rather than to invent a price out of it. Deciding what an impossible case should do, before it ever happens, is the cheapest debugging there is - it is the fault you never have to reproduce.

independent-practice.prompt: A friend messages you: `your program is broken, it crashed`. That is the whole message. Describe what you ask for and what you do before you change a single line, and explain why editing something straight away is the worse move.
independent-practice.explain: The half that people skip is the second one: without a case that fails every time, a change that appears to work has proved nothing, because you never saw it fail to begin with. Asking for the exact input and the exact message costs one reply and turns a rumour into something you can run, and the message alone often names the fault before you have opened the file.

exam.prompt: What does the last line of a Python traceback tell you?
choices: The first line of the program that ran
The kind of failure, and a short message describing it
The number of the line at which the program stopped
Which names still had values when the program stopped
exam.explain: The third choice is tempting because a line number really is in there - one line further up, on the line beginning `File`. Keeping the two apart matters, because the bottom line says what kind of wrong value was involved, and that is what tells you which sort of earlier line to suspect.

exam.prompt: Which of these faults are found before any line of the program runs? Select every one.
choices: a missing colon at the end of an `if` line
dividing by a count that turned out to be zero
an opening bracket that is never closed
reading a name that was never assigned
exam.explain: The fourth is the one that lands in the wrong pile, because a misspelt name looks like the same sort of slip as a misspelt keyword. It is not: `whlie` cannot be read as legal Python at all, whereas a misspelt name is a perfectly legal name that merely has nothing attached to it, so nobody finds out until that line runs.

exam.prompt: Give the name Python reports in each of these four situations. Spell each one exactly as Python does.
exam.template:
joining a number to a piece of text with +: ___
asking int for the number in the text "nine": ___
using a name that was never assigned: ___
dividing by a count that turned out to be zero: ___
exam.explain: The second is the one that gets answered with the first. Text is exactly the kind of thing `int` is built to take, so nothing about the type is wrong; the complaint is about the characters inside it, and Python quotes them back at you in the message for precisely that reason.

exam.prompt: A probe has been added to this loop. What does the program print? Write all four lines.
exam.code:
total = 0
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print("probe n", n, "total", total)
    total = total + n
    n = n - 1
print("total", total)
exam.answer:
probe n 3 total 0
probe n 2 total 3
probe n 1 total 5
total 6
exam.explain: The probe sits above the addition, so each line shows the running total as it was on entering the pass rather than after it - which is why the last probe says 5 while the answer is 6. A probe that reports the state before the work is usually the more useful of the two, because it shows you what the pass was given.

exam.prompt: Somebody reports that a program gives a wrong answer. Put these five actions into the order that finds the fault soonest.
fragments: Run it on the exact input that was reported, and watch it come out wrong
Print the values roughly halfway through, and see whether they are wrong there already
Move the probe into whichever half still holds the fault
Run the same input again and compare
exam.explain: Every wrong order puts a change before a measurement, which is the habit this floor exists to break. Reproducing first is what makes the final comparison mean anything: if you never saw it fail, a run that succeeds afterwards is no evidence that you fixed it.

exam.prompt: A probe has been placed at the end of each pass of this loop. Give the values it would report.

steps.label: n, at the end of pass 1
n, at the end of pass 2
n, at the end of pass 3
count, at the end of pass 3

exam.explain: Tracing by hand and probing with `print` are the same act performed by different machinery, and doing it by hand first is what lets you notice when the printed values disagree with you. The trap here is the very first pass: 5 is odd, so the number grows before it ever shrinks.

exam.prompt: This program reads a whole number of coins and should print `you have 12 coins` for the typed line `12`. It stops with a traceback whose last line names something the program never assigned. Repair it.
exam.explain: A `NameError` is the one failure whose message hands you the answer verbatim: it prints the name it could not find, and a name one letter away from a name you did assign is a typo nine times out of ten. Read the quoted name rather than the line, because the line itself looks perfectly reasonable.

exam.prompt: This program reads a whole number and should print how many of the numbers from 1 up to and including it divide it exactly, so for the typed line `6` it prints `4`, counting 1, 2, 3 and 6. It reports no error and prints `3`. Repair it.
exam.starterCode:
n = int(input())
found = 0
d = 1
while d < n:
    if n % d == 0:
        found = found + 1
    d = d + 1
print(found)
exam.solution:
n = int(input())
found = 0
d = 1
while d <= n:
    if n % d == 0:
        found = found + 1
    d = d + 1
print(found)
exam.explain: Being short by exactly one for every input points at the range rather than at the test inside it, and a probe printing `d` on each pass shows in a single run that the largest divisor is never even offered. The `1` case is the cruel one: the broken program prints 0 for it, so a repair that merely adds one to the answer passes for 6 and fails here.

exam.prompt: Write a program that reads one typed line holding a whole number and prints every whole number from it down to 1, each on its own line, followed by a final line reading `done`. For the typed line `3` it prints `3`, `2`, `1`, `done`. For the typed line `0` it prints only `done`.
exam.starterCode:
n = int(input())
# Count down to 1, then print done.
exam.solution:
n = int(input())
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
print("done")
exam.hint: Decide first what should happen when the typed number is already below 1, and check that case before you check the ordinary one.
exam.explain: The boundaries are the whole exercise: a version that stops one pass too late prints a `0`, and one that stops a pass too early never prints the `1`, and both are a single character adrift in the condition. Running the `1` case is quicker than reasoning about it, and that habit is the thing worth carrying off this floor.

exam.prompt: A program gives a wrong answer and reports no error at all. Somebody edits four lines at once, runs it, and gets a different wrong answer. Explain what has been lost by working that way, and describe how you would corner the fault instead.
exam.explain: What is lost is not the four lines, which can be typed again, but the knowledge of which of them mattered - and worse, the program is now a different program, so the original evidence no longer describes it. Printing values and moving one line at a time is slower per step and far faster overall, because every step rules something out permanently.
